title: HE HAD EVERYTHING… AND STILL LOST GOD?
paragraphs:
HE HAD EVERYTHING… AND STILL LOST GOD?
The Chilling Truth About Solomon’s Final Days That Most Believers Ignore
There is something deeply unsettling about the end of Solomon’s life.
But because of how quietly he drifted.

No sudden collapse.
No dramatic rebellion.
No public renunciation of God.

Just a slow, almost unnoticeable turning…
until the man who once built the temple of God began building altars for idols.
And if that doesn’t shake you… it should.

Because Solomon didn’t start weak.
He started as one of the most spiritually favored men to ever live.
When God asked him what he desired, Solomon didn’t ask for wealth, power, or revenge. He asked for wisdom.
In Hebrew, he asked for “לֵב שֹׁמֵעַ” (lev shomea) — a listening heart (1 Kings 3:9).
A heart that leans toward heaven.
So pleased that He gave Solomon not only wisdom, but wealth, honor, influence, and peace unlike any king before or after him.

“וַיִּתֵּן אֱלֹהִים חָכְמָה לִשְׁלֹמֹה”
“And God gave wisdom to Solomon…”

He wrote Proverbs.
He composed songs.
He spoke mysteries of life, nature, justice, and the human soul.
People traveled from nations away just to hear him speak.
And yet… something began to shift.
Just slowly enough that it didn’t feel dangerous.
“Now King Solomon loved many foreign women…”
And God had already warned Israel clearly in Deuteronomy 7:3–4 that these unions would turn hearts away.
The Hebrew phrase used in 1 Kings 11:2 is piercing:
Because once the heart shifts… everything follows.
This is the same man who once asked for a listening heart.
Now his heart is no longer listening to God.
You can still sound wise… and be far from God.
You can still lead… and be spiritually drifting.
You can still be admired… and be internally compromised.
Solomon began building high places for Chemosh, Molech, and other detestable gods.
The man who built the temple… built altars to demons.
Through quiet disobedience that didn’t seem urgent at the time.

“וַיִּתְאַנַּף יְהוָה בִּשְׁלֹמֹה”
“The LORD became angry with Solomon…”
“Because his heart had turned away from the LORD.”
Not because he didn’t know better.
But because he did… and still drifted.
God had appeared to him twice.
How do you walk away after that?
The same way many still do today.
By letting other loves take His place.
By slowly giving your heart to things that were never meant to hold it.
And yet… this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because many scholars believe Ecclesiastes was written at the end of Solomon’s life.
And if that’s true… then what we are reading is not just philosophy.
It’s a man who tasted everything the world offers… and found it empty.

“הֲבֵל הֲבָלִים… הַכֹּל הָבֶל” (hevel havalim… hakol havel)
“Vanity of vanities… all is vanity.”
The word “hevel” doesn’t just mean meaningless.
Something that disappears the moment you try to grasp it.
“I had it all… and it slipped through my hands.”
None of it filled the void.
And at the very end… after everything…
And maybe you’re reading this right now feeling something uncomfortable.
your heart has been drifting too.
you’re not as close as you used to be.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because this is not about condemning Solomon.
It’s about recognizing ourselves in his story.
And realizing… we don’t have to end the same way.
Jesus didn’t come for perfect people.
For those who slowly lost their way… and didn’t even realize it.
The Gospel is not just about forgiveness.
Because where Solomon failed… Jesus remained faithful.
Where Solomon’s heart turned… Jesus’ heart stayed surrendered.
Where Solomon chased everything… Jesus gave everything.
Let this not just be something you read.
Let it be something that changes you.
It’s about becoming someone who finishes well.
but his ending became a warning.
Come back while your heart is still listening.
Because the most dangerous distance from God… is the one you don’t notice forming.
